# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/src/cpp/lib.rs.html

# cpp/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![allow(clippy::needless_doctest_main)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! This crate `cpp` provides macros that allow embedding arbitrary C++ code.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! # Usage
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! This crate must be used in tandem with the [`cpp_build`](https://docs.rs/cpp_build) crate. A basic Cargo
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! project which uses these projects would have a structure like the following:
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ```text
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! crate
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! |-- Cargo.toml
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! |-- src
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     |-- main.rs
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! |-- build.rs
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Where the files look like the following:
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! #### Cargo.toml
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```toml
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! [package]
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! build = "build.rs"
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [dependencies]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! cpp = "0.5"
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [build-dependencies]
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! cpp_build = "0.5"
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! ```
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! #### build.rs
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```no_run
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! extern crate cpp_build;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! fn main() {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     cpp_build::build("src/main.rs");
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! ```
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! #### main.rs
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ```ignore
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! # // tested in test/src/examples.rs
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! use cpp::cpp;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! cpp!{{
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!     #include <iostream>
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! }}
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! fn main() {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!     let name = std::ffi::CString::new("World").unwrap();
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     let name_ptr = name.as_ptr();
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     let r = unsafe {
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!         cpp!([name_ptr as "const char *"] -> u32 as "int32_t" {
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!             std::cout << "Hello, " << name_ptr << std::endl;
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!             return 42;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!         })
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!     };
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     assert_eq!(r, 42)
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! }
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! # Build script
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! Use the `cpp_build` crates from your `build.rs` script.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! The same version of `cpp_build` and `cpp` crates should be used.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! You can simply use the `cpp_build::build` function, or the `cpp_build::Config`
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! struct if you want more option.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! Behind the scene, it uses the `cc` crate.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ## Using external libraries
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! Most likely you will want to link against external libraries. You need to tell cpp_build
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! about the include path and other flags via `cpp_build::Config` and you need to let cargo
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! know about the link. More info in the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html).
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! Your `build.rs` could look like this:
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ```no_run
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! fn main() {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     let include_path = "/usr/include/myexternallib";
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     let lib_path = "/usr/lib/myexternallib";
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!     cpp_build::Config::new().include(include_path).build("src/lib.rs");
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     println!("cargo:rustc-link-search={}", lib_path);
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=myexternallib");
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! ```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! (But you probably want to allow to configure the path via environment variables or
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! find them using some external tool such as the `pkg-config` crate, instead of hardcoding
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! them in the source)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! # Limitations
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! As with all procedure macro crates we also need to parse Rust source files to
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! extract C++ code. That leads to the fact that some of the language features
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! might not be supported in full. One example is the attributes. Only a limited
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! number of attributes is supported, namely: `#[path = "..."]` for `mod`
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! declarations to specify an alternative path to the module file and
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! `#[cfg(feature = "...")]` for `mod` declarations to conditionally include the
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! module into the parsing process. Please note that the latter is only supported
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! in its simplest form: straight-forward `feature = "..."` without any
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! additional conditions, `cfg!` macros are also not supported at the moment.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! Since the C++ code is included within a rust file, the C++ code must obey both
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! the Rust and the C++ lexing rules. For example, Rust supports nested block comments
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! (`/* ... /* ... */ ... */`) while C++ does not, so nested comments not be used in the
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! `cpp!` macro. Also the Rust lexer will not understand the C++ raw literal, nor all
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! the C++ escape sequences within literal, so only string literals that are both valid
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! in Rust and in C++ should be used. The same applies for group separators in numbers.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! Be careful to properly use `#if` / `#else` / `#endif`, and not have unbalanced delimiters.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)
[115](https://docs.rs#115)#![no_std]
[116](https://docs.rs#116)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)#[macro_use]
[118](https://docs.rs#118)#[allow(unused_imports)]
[119](https://docs.rs#119)extern crate cpp_macros;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)#[doc(hidden)]
[121](https://docs.rs#121)pub use cpp_macros::*;
[122](https://docs.rs#122)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// Internal macro which is used to locate the `rust!` invocations in the
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// C++ code embedded in `cpp!` invocation, to translate them into `extern`
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// functions
[126](https://docs.rs#126)#[doc(hidden)]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)#[macro_export]
[128](https://docs.rs#128)macro_rules! __cpp_internal {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] rust!($($rust_body:tt)*) $($rest:tt)*) => {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @expand_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rust_body)* }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rest)* }
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    };
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] ( $($in:tt)* ) $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] [ $($in:tt)* ] $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] { $($in:tt)* } $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $t:tt $($rest:tt)*) =>
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rest)* } };
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*]) => {};
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    (@expand_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $i:ident [$($an:ident : $at:ty as $ac:tt),*] {$($body:tt)*}) => {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        #[allow(non_snake_case)]
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        #[allow(unused_unsafe)]
[146](https://docs.rs#146)        #[allow(clippy::forget_copy, clippy::forget_ref)]
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        #[doc(hidden)]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        $($a)* unsafe extern "C" fn $i($($an : *const $at),*) {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            $(let $an : $at = unsafe { $an.read() };)*
[150](https://docs.rs#150)            (|| { $($body)* })();
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            $(::core::mem::forget($an);)*
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    };
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    (@expand_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $i:ident [$($an:ident : $at:ty as $ac:tt),*] -> $rt:ty as $rc:tt {$($body:tt)*}) => {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        #[allow(non_snake_case)]
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        #[allow(unused_unsafe)]
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        #[allow(clippy::forget_copy, clippy::forget_ref)]
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        #[doc(hidden)]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        $($a)* unsafe extern "C" fn $i($($an : *const $at, )* rt : *mut $rt) -> *mut $rt {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            $(let $an : $at = unsafe { $an.read() };)*
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)                #[allow(unused_mut)]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)                let mut lambda = || {$($body)*};
[166](https://docs.rs#166)                unsafe { ::core::ptr::write(rt, lambda()) };
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            $(::core::mem::forget($an);)*
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            rt
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    };
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    (@expand_rust_macro $($invalid:tt)*) => {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        compile_error!(concat!( "Cannot parse rust! macro: ", stringify!([ $($invalid)* ]) ))
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    };
[176](https://docs.rs#176)}
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// This macro is used to embed arbitrary C++ code.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// There are two variants of the `cpp!` macro. The first variant is used for
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// raw text inclusion. Text is included into the generated `C++` file in the
[182](https://docs.rs#182)/// order which they were defined, inlining module declarations.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// ```ignore
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// cpp! {{
[186](https://docs.rs#186)///     #include <stdint.h>
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///     #include <stdio.h>
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// }}
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// ```
[190](https://docs.rs#190)///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// The second variant is used to embed C++ code within Rust code. A list of
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// variable names which should be captured are taken as the first argument,
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// with their corresponding C++ type. The body is compiled as a C++ function.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// This variant of the macro may only be invoked in expression context, and
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// requires an `unsafe` block, as it is performing FFI.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// ```ignore
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// let y: i32 = 10;
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// let mut z: i32 = 20;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// let x: i32 = unsafe { cpp!([y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///     z++;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)///     return y + z;
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// })};
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// ```
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// You can also put the unsafe keyword as the first keyword of the `cpp!` macro, which
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// has the same effect as putting the whole macro in an `unsafe` block:
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// ```ignore
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// let x: i32 = cpp!(unsafe [y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///     z++;
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///     return y + z;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// });
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)///
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// ## rust! pseudo-macro
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// The `cpp!` macro can contain, in the C++ code, a `rust!` sub-macro, which allows
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// the inclusion of Rust code in C++ code. This is useful to
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// implement callback or override virtual functions. Example:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// ```ignore
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// trait MyTrait {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///    fn compute_value(&self, x : i32) -> i32;
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// }
[227](https://docs.rs#227)///
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// cpp!{{
[229](https://docs.rs#229)///    struct TraitPtr { void *a,*b; };
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///    class MyClassImpl : public MyClass {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)///      public:
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///        TraitPtr m_trait;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)///        int computeValue(int x) const override {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)///            return rust!(MCI_computeValue [m_trait : &MyTrait as "TraitPtr", x : i32 as "int"]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)///                -> i32 as "int" {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)///                m_trait.compute_value(x)
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///            });
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///        }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)///    }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// }}
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// ```
[242](https://docs.rs#242)///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// The syntax for the `rust!` macro is:
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// ```ignore
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// rust!($uniq_ident:ident [$($arg_name:ident : $arg_rust_type:ty as $arg_c_type:tt),*]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///      $(-> $ret_rust_type:ty as $rust_c_type:tt)* {$($body:tt)*})
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// `uniq_ident` is a unique identifier which will be used to name the `extern` function
[249](https://docs.rs#249)#[macro_export]
[250](https://docs.rs#250)macro_rules! cpp {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    // raw text inclusion
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ({$($body:tt)*}) => { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [#[no_mangle] pub] $($body)*} };
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    // inline closure
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ([$($captures:tt)*] $($rest:tt)*) => {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)            $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [] $($rest)*}
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            #[allow(unused)]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            #[derive($crate::__cpp_internal_closure)]
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            enum CppClosureInput {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                Input = (stringify!([$($captures)*] $($rest)*), 0).1
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            __cpp_closure_impl![$($captures)*]
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    };
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    // wrap unsafe
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    (unsafe $($tail:tt)*) => { unsafe { cpp!($($tail)*) } };
[269](https://docs.rs#269)}
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)#[doc(hidden)]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)pub trait CppTrait {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    type BaseType;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    const ARRAY_SIZE: usize;
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    const CPP_TYPE: &'static str;
[276](https://docs.rs#276)}
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// This macro allows wrapping a relocatable C++ struct or class that might have
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// a destructor or copy constructor, implementing the `Drop` and `Clone` trait
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// appropriately.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// ```ignore
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// cpp_class!(pub unsafe struct MyClass as "MyClass");
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// impl MyClass {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///     fn new() -> Self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///         unsafe { cpp!([] -> MyClass as "MyClass" { return MyClass(); }) }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)///     }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///     fn member_function(&self, param : i32) -> i32 {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)///         unsafe { cpp!([self as "const MyClass*", param as "int"] -> i32 as "int" {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///             return self->member_function(param);
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///         }) }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///     }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// ```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// This will create a Rust struct `MyClass`, which has the same size and
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// alignment as the C++ class `MyClass`. It will also implement the `Drop` trait
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// calling the destructor, the `Clone` trait calling the copy constructor, if the
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// class is copyable (or `Copy` if it is trivially copyable), and `Default` if the class
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// is default constructible
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// ## Derived Traits
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// The `Default`, `Clone` and `Copy` traits are implicitly implemented if the C++
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// type has the corresponding constructors.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// You can add the `#[derive(...)]` attribute in the macro in order to get automatic
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// implementation of the following traits:
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// * The trait `PartialEq` will call the C++ `operator==`.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// * You can add the trait `Eq` if the semantics of the C++ operator are those of `Eq`
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// * The trait `PartialOrd` need the C++ `operator<` for that type. `lt`, `le`, `gt` and
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///   `ge` will use the corresponding C++ operator if it is defined, otherwise it will
[314](https://docs.rs#314)///   fallback to the less than operator. For PartialOrd::partial_cmp, the `operator<` will
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///   be called twice. Note that it will never return `None`.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// * The trait `Ord` can also be specified when the semantics of the `operator<` corresponds
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///   to a total order
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// ## Safety Warning
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// Use of this macro is highly unsafe. Only certain C++ classes can be bound
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// to, C++ classes may perform arbitrary unsafe operations, and invariants are
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// easy to break.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// A notable restriction is that this macro only works if the C++ class is
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// relocatable.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// ## Relocatable classes
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// In order to be able to we wrapped the C++ class must be relocatable. That means
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// that it can be moved in memory using `memcpy`. This restriction exists because
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// safe Rust is allowed to move your types around.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)///
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// Most C++ types which do not contain self-references will be compatible,
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// although this property cannot be statically checked by `rust-cpp`.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// All types that satisfy `std::is_trivially_copyable` are compatible.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)/// Maybe future version of the C++ standard would allow a compile-time check:
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// [P1144](http://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p1144r4.html)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// Unfortunately, as the STL often uses internal self-references for
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// optimization purposes, such as the small-string optimization, this disallows
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// most std:: classes.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// But `std::unique_ptr<T>` and `std::shared_ptr<T>` works.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)#[macro_export]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)macro_rules! cpp_class {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    };
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [pub] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    };
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub($($pub:tt)*) unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [pub($($pub)*)] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    };
[356](https://docs.rs#356)}
[357](https://docs.rs#357)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// Implementation details for cpp_class!
[359](https://docs.rs#359)#[doc(hidden)]
[360](https://docs.rs#360)#[macro_export]
[361](https://docs.rs#361)macro_rules! __cpp_class_internal {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    (@parse [$($attrs:tt)*] [$($vis:tt)*] [unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr]) => {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes [ $($attrs)* ] [] [
[364](https://docs.rs#364)            #[derive($crate::__cpp_internal_class)]
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            #[repr(C)]
[366](https://docs.rs#366)            $($vis)* struct $name {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                _opaque : [<$name as $crate::CppTrait>::BaseType ; <$name as $crate::CppTrait>::ARRAY_SIZE
[368](https://docs.rs#368)                    + (stringify!($($attrs)* $($vis)* unsafe struct $name as $type), 0).1]
[369](https://docs.rs#369)            }
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        ]}
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    };
[372](https://docs.rs#372)
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    (@parse_attributes [] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*]) => ( $($attributes)* $($result)* );
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    (@parse_attributes [#[derive($($der:ident),*)] $($tail:tt)* ] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*] )
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($der),*] @parse_attributes [$($tail)*] [ $($attributes)* ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    (@parse_attributes [ #[$m:meta] $($tail:tt)* ] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*])
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes [$($tail)*] [$($attributes)* #[$m] ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    (@parse_derive [] @parse_attributes $($result:tt)*) => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes $($result)*} );
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    (@parse_derive [PartialEq $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    (@parse_derive [PartialOrd $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    (@parse_derive [Ord $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    (@parse_derive [Default $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    (@parse_derive [Clone $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    (@parse_derive [Copy $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    (@parse_derive [$i:ident $(,$tail:ident)*] @parse_attributes [$($attr:tt)*] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*] )
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] @parse_attributes [$($attr)*] [$($attributes)* #[derive($i)] ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[394](https://docs.rs#394)}

# cpp in cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/cpp/macro.cpp.html

```
macro_rules! cpp {
    ({$($body:tt)*}) => { ... };
    ([$($captures:tt)*] $($rest:tt)*) => { ... };
    (unsafe $($tail:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

This macro is used to embed arbitrary C++ code.

There are two variants of the `cpp!` macro. The first variant is used for
raw text inclusion. Text is included into the generated `C++` file in the
order which they were defined, inlining module declarations.

The second variant is used to embed C++ code within Rust code. A list of variable names which should be captured are taken as the first argument, with their corresponding C++ type. The body is compiled as a C++ function.

This variant of the macro may only be invoked in expression context, and
requires an `unsafe` block, as it is performing FFI.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let y: i32 = 10;
let mut z: i32 = 20;
let x: i32 = unsafe { cpp!([y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
    z++;
    return y + z;
})};
```
You can also put the unsafe keyword as the first keyword of the `cpp!` macro, which
has the same effect as putting the whole macro in an `unsafe` block:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let x: i32 = cpp!(unsafe [y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
    z++;
    return y + z;
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-pseudo-macro)rust! pseudo-macro

The `cpp!` macro can contain, in the C++ code, a `rust!` sub-macro, which allows
the inclusion of Rust code in C++ code. This is useful to
implement callback or override virtual functions. Example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
trait MyTrait {
   fn compute_value(&self, x : i32) -> i32;
}
cpp!{{
   struct TraitPtr { void *a,*b; };
   class MyClassImpl : public MyClass {
     public:
       TraitPtr m_trait;
       int computeValue(int x) const override {
           return rust!(MCI_computeValue [m_trait : &MyTrait as "TraitPtr", x : i32 as "int"]
               -> i32 as "int" {
               m_trait.compute_value(x)
           });
       }
   }
}}
```
The syntax for the `rust!` macro is:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
rust!($uniq_ident:ident [$($arg_name:ident : $arg_rust_type:ty as $arg_c_type:tt),*]
     $(-> $ret_rust_type:ty as $rust_c_type:tt)* {$($body:tt)*})
```
`uniq_ident` is a unique identifier which will be used to name the `extern` function

---

# cpp_class in cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/cpp/macro.cpp_class.html

```
macro_rules! cpp_class {
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub($($pub:tt)*) unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

This macro allows wrapping a relocatable C++ struct or class that might have
a destructor or copy constructor, implementing the `Drop` and `Clone` trait
appropriately.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
cpp_class!(pub unsafe struct MyClass as "MyClass");
impl MyClass {
    fn new() -> Self {
        unsafe { cpp!([] -> MyClass as "MyClass" { return MyClass(); }) }
    }
    fn member_function(&self, param : i32) -> i32 {
        unsafe { cpp!([self as "const MyClass*", param as "int"] -> i32 as "int" {
            return self->member_function(param);
        }) }
    }
}
```
This will create a Rust struct `MyClass`, which has the same size and
alignment as the C++ class `MyClass`. It will also implement the `Drop` trait
calling the destructor, the `Clone` trait calling the copy constructor, if the
class is copyable (or `Copy` if it is trivially copyable), and `Default` if the class
is default constructible

[§](https://docs.rs#derived-traits)Derived Traits

The `Default`, `Clone` and `Copy` traits are implicitly implemented if the C++
type has the corresponding constructors.

You can add the `#[derive(...)]` attribute in the macro in order to get automatic
implementation of the following traits:

- The trait `PartialEq`will call the C++`operator==`.
- You can add the trait `Eq`if the semantics of the C++ operator are those of`Eq`
- The trait `PartialOrd`need the C++`operator<`for that type.`lt`,`le`,`gt`and`ge`will use the corresponding C++ operator if it is defined, otherwise it will fallback to the less than operator. For PartialOrd::partial_cmp, the`operator<`will be called twice. Note that it will never return`None`.
- The trait `Ord`can also be specified when the semantics of the`operator<`corresponds to a total order

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-warning)Safety Warning

Use of this macro is highly unsafe. Only certain C++ classes can be bound to, C++ classes may perform arbitrary unsafe operations, and invariants are easy to break.

A notable restriction is that this macro only works if the C++ class is relocatable.

[§](https://docs.rs#relocatable-classes)Relocatable classes

In order to be able to we wrapped the C++ class must be relocatable. That means
that it can be moved in memory using `memcpy`. This restriction exists because
safe Rust is allowed to move your types around.

Most C++ types which do not contain self-references will be compatible,
although this property cannot be statically checked by `rust-cpp`.
All types that satisfy `std::is_trivially_copyable` are compatible.
Maybe future version of the C++ standard would allow a compile-time check:
[P1144](http://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p1144r4.html)

Unfortunately, as the STL often uses internal self-references for
optimization purposes, such as the small-string optimization, this disallows
most std:: classes.
But `std::unique_ptr<T>` and `std::shared_ptr<T>` works.

---

# cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpp/0.5.11/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cpp/

## Expand description

This crate `cpp` provides macros that allow embedding arbitrary C++ code.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This crate must be used in tandem with the [ cpp_build](https://docs.rs/cpp_build) crate. A basic Cargo
project which uses these projects would have a structure like the following:

```
crate
|-- Cargo.toml
|-- src
    |-- main.rs
|-- build.rs
```
Where the files look like the following:

[§](https://docs.rs#cargotoml)Cargo.toml

```
[package]
build = "build.rs"
[dependencies]
cpp = "0.5"
[build-dependencies]
cpp_build = "0.5"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs)build.rs

```
extern crate cpp_build;
fn main() {
    cpp_build::build("src/main.rs");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mainrs)main.rs

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use cpp::cpp;
cpp!{{
    #include <iostream>
}}
fn main() {
    let name = std::ffi::CString::new("World").unwrap();
    let name_ptr = name.as_ptr();
    let r = unsafe {
        cpp!([name_ptr as "const char *"] -> u32 as "int32_t" {
            std::cout << "Hello, " << name_ptr << std::endl;
            return 42;
        })
    };
    assert_eq!(r, 42)
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#build-script)Build script

Use the `cpp_build` crates from your `build.rs` script.
The same version of `cpp_build` and `cpp` crates should be used.
You can simply use the `cpp_build::build` function, or the `cpp_build::Config`
struct if you want more option.

Behind the scene, it uses the `cc` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-external-libraries)Using external libraries

Most likely you will want to link against external libraries. You need to tell cpp_build
about the include path and other flags via `cpp_build::Config` and you need to let cargo
know about the link. More info in the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html).

Your `build.rs` could look like this:

```
fn main() {
    let include_path = "/usr/include/myexternallib";
    let lib_path = "/usr/lib/myexternallib";
    cpp_build::Config::new().include(include_path).build("src/lib.rs");
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-search={}", lib_path);
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=myexternallib");
}
```
(But you probably want to allow to configure the path via environment variables or
find them using some external tool such as the `pkg-config` crate, instead of hardcoding
them in the source)

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

As with all procedure macro crates we also need to parse Rust source files to
extract C++ code. That leads to the fact that some of the language features
might not be supported in full. One example is the attributes. Only a limited
number of attributes is supported, namely: `#[path = "..."]` for `mod`
declarations to specify an alternative path to the module file and
`#[cfg(feature = "...")]` for `mod` declarations to conditionally include the
module into the parsing process. Please note that the latter is only supported
in its simplest form: straight-forward `feature = "..."` without any
additional conditions, `cfg!` macros are also not supported at the moment.

Since the C++ code is included within a rust file, the C++ code must obey both
the Rust and the C++ lexing rules. For example, Rust supports nested block comments
(`/* ... /* ... */ ... */`) while C++ does not, so nested comments not be used in the
`cpp!` macro. Also the Rust lexer will not understand the C++ raw literal, nor all
the C++ escape sequences within literal, so only string literals that are both valid
in Rust and in C++ should be used. The same applies for group separators in numbers.
Be careful to properly use `#if` / `#else` / `#endif`, and not have unbalanced delimiters.

---

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/src/cpp/lib.rs.html

# cpp/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![allow(clippy::needless_doctest_main)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! This crate `cpp` provides macros that allow embedding arbitrary C++ code.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! # Usage
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! This crate must be used in tandem with the [`cpp_build`](https://docs.rs/cpp_build) crate. A basic Cargo
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! project which uses these projects would have a structure like the following:
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ```text
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! crate
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! |-- Cargo.toml
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! |-- src
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     |-- main.rs
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! |-- build.rs
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Where the files look like the following:
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! #### Cargo.toml
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```toml
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! [package]
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! build = "build.rs"
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [dependencies]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! cpp = "0.5"
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [build-dependencies]
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! cpp_build = "0.5"
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! ```
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! #### build.rs
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```no_run
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! extern crate cpp_build;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! fn main() {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     cpp_build::build("src/main.rs");
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! ```
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! #### main.rs
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ```ignore
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! # // tested in test/src/examples.rs
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! use cpp::cpp;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! cpp!{{
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!     #include <iostream>
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! }}
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! fn main() {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!     let name = std::ffi::CString::new("World").unwrap();
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     let name_ptr = name.as_ptr();
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     let r = unsafe {
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!         cpp!([name_ptr as "const char *"] -> u32 as "int32_t" {
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!             std::cout << "Hello, " << name_ptr << std::endl;
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!             return 42;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!         })
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!     };
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     assert_eq!(r, 42)
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! }
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! # Build script
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! Use the `cpp_build` crates from your `build.rs` script.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! The same version of `cpp_build` and `cpp` crates should be used.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! You can simply use the `cpp_build::build` function, or the `cpp_build::Config`
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! struct if you want more option.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! Behind the scene, it uses the `cc` crate.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ## Using external libraries
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! Most likely you will want to link against external libraries. You need to tell cpp_build
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! about the include path and other flags via `cpp_build::Config` and you need to let cargo
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! know about the link. More info in the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html).
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! Your `build.rs` could look like this:
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ```no_run
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! fn main() {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     let include_path = "/usr/include/myexternallib";
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     let lib_path = "/usr/lib/myexternallib";
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!     cpp_build::Config::new().include(include_path).build("src/lib.rs");
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     println!("cargo:rustc-link-search={}", lib_path);
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=myexternallib");
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! ```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! (But you probably want to allow to configure the path via environment variables or
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! find them using some external tool such as the `pkg-config` crate, instead of hardcoding
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! them in the source)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! # Limitations
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! As with all procedure macro crates we also need to parse Rust source files to
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! extract C++ code. That leads to the fact that some of the language features
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! might not be supported in full. One example is the attributes. Only a limited
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! number of attributes is supported, namely: `#[path = "..."]` for `mod`
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! declarations to specify an alternative path to the module file and
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! `#[cfg(feature = "...")]` for `mod` declarations to conditionally include the
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! module into the parsing process. Please note that the latter is only supported
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! in its simplest form: straight-forward `feature = "..."` without any
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! additional conditions, `cfg!` macros are also not supported at the moment.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! Since the C++ code is included within a rust file, the C++ code must obey both
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! the Rust and the C++ lexing rules. For example, Rust supports nested block comments
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! (`/* ... /* ... */ ... */`) while C++ does not, so nested comments not be used in the
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! `cpp!` macro. Also the Rust lexer will not understand the C++ raw literal, nor all
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! the C++ escape sequences within literal, so only string literals that are both valid
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! in Rust and in C++ should be used. The same applies for group separators in numbers.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! Be careful to properly use `#if` / `#else` / `#endif`, and not have unbalanced delimiters.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)
[115](https://docs.rs#115)#![no_std]
[116](https://docs.rs#116)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)#[macro_use]
[118](https://docs.rs#118)#[allow(unused_imports)]
[119](https://docs.rs#119)extern crate cpp_macros;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)#[doc(hidden)]
[121](https://docs.rs#121)pub use cpp_macros::*;
[122](https://docs.rs#122)
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// Internal macro which is used to locate the `rust!` invocations in the
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// C++ code embedded in `cpp!` invocation, to translate them into `extern`
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// functions
[126](https://docs.rs#126)#[doc(hidden)]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)#[macro_export]
[128](https://docs.rs#128)macro_rules! __cpp_internal {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] rust!($($rust_body:tt)*) $($rest:tt)*) => {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @expand_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rust_body)* }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rest)* }
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    };
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] ( $($in:tt)* ) $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] [ $($in:tt)* ] $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] { $($in:tt)* } $($rest:tt)* ) =>
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($in)* $($rest)* }  };
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $t:tt $($rest:tt)*) =>
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [$($a)*] $($rest)* } };
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    (@find_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*]) => {};
[142](https://docs.rs#142)
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    (@expand_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $i:ident [$($an:ident : $at:ty as $ac:tt),*] {$($body:tt)*}) => {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        #[allow(non_snake_case)]
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        #[allow(unused_unsafe)]
[146](https://docs.rs#146)        #[allow(clippy::forget_copy, clippy::forget_ref)]
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        #[doc(hidden)]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        $($a)* unsafe extern "C" fn $i($($an : *const $at),*) {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            $(let $an : $at = unsafe { $an.read() };)*
[150](https://docs.rs#150)            (|| { $($body)* })();
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            $(::core::mem::forget($an);)*
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    };
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    (@expand_rust_macro [$($a:tt)*] $i:ident [$($an:ident : $at:ty as $ac:tt),*] -> $rt:ty as $rc:tt {$($body:tt)*}) => {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        #[allow(non_snake_case)]
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        #[allow(unused_unsafe)]
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        #[allow(clippy::forget_copy, clippy::forget_ref)]
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        #[doc(hidden)]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        $($a)* unsafe extern "C" fn $i($($an : *const $at, )* rt : *mut $rt) -> *mut $rt {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            $(let $an : $at = unsafe { $an.read() };)*
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            {
[164](https://docs.rs#164)                #[allow(unused_mut)]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)                let mut lambda = || {$($body)*};
[166](https://docs.rs#166)                unsafe { ::core::ptr::write(rt, lambda()) };
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            $(::core::mem::forget($an);)*
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            rt
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    };
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    (@expand_rust_macro $($invalid:tt)*) => {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        compile_error!(concat!( "Cannot parse rust! macro: ", stringify!([ $($invalid)* ]) ))
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    };
[176](https://docs.rs#176)}
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// This macro is used to embed arbitrary C++ code.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// There are two variants of the `cpp!` macro. The first variant is used for
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// raw text inclusion. Text is included into the generated `C++` file in the
[182](https://docs.rs#182)/// order which they were defined, inlining module declarations.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// ```ignore
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// cpp! {{
[186](https://docs.rs#186)///     #include <stdint.h>
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///     #include <stdio.h>
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// }}
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// ```
[190](https://docs.rs#190)///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// The second variant is used to embed C++ code within Rust code. A list of
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// variable names which should be captured are taken as the first argument,
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// with their corresponding C++ type. The body is compiled as a C++ function.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// This variant of the macro may only be invoked in expression context, and
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// requires an `unsafe` block, as it is performing FFI.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// ```ignore
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// let y: i32 = 10;
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// let mut z: i32 = 20;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// let x: i32 = unsafe { cpp!([y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///     z++;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)///     return y + z;
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// })};
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// ```
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// You can also put the unsafe keyword as the first keyword of the `cpp!` macro, which
[208](https://docs.rs#208)/// has the same effect as putting the whole macro in an `unsafe` block:
[209](https://docs.rs#209)///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// ```ignore
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// let x: i32 = cpp!(unsafe [y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///     z++;
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///     return y + z;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// });
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)///
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// ## rust! pseudo-macro
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// The `cpp!` macro can contain, in the C++ code, a `rust!` sub-macro, which allows
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// the inclusion of Rust code in C++ code. This is useful to
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// implement callback or override virtual functions. Example:
[222](https://docs.rs#222)///
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// ```ignore
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// trait MyTrait {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///    fn compute_value(&self, x : i32) -> i32;
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// }
[227](https://docs.rs#227)///
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// cpp!{{
[229](https://docs.rs#229)///    struct TraitPtr { void *a,*b; };
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///    class MyClassImpl : public MyClass {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)///      public:
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///        TraitPtr m_trait;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)///        int computeValue(int x) const override {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)///            return rust!(MCI_computeValue [m_trait : &MyTrait as "TraitPtr", x : i32 as "int"]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)///                -> i32 as "int" {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)///                m_trait.compute_value(x)
[237](https://docs.rs#237)///            });
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///        }
[239](https://docs.rs#239)///    }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// }}
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// ```
[242](https://docs.rs#242)///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// The syntax for the `rust!` macro is:
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// ```ignore
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// rust!($uniq_ident:ident [$($arg_name:ident : $arg_rust_type:ty as $arg_c_type:tt),*]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)///      $(-> $ret_rust_type:ty as $rust_c_type:tt)* {$($body:tt)*})
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// `uniq_ident` is a unique identifier which will be used to name the `extern` function
[249](https://docs.rs#249)#[macro_export]
[250](https://docs.rs#250)macro_rules! cpp {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    // raw text inclusion
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    ({$($body:tt)*}) => { $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [#[no_mangle] pub] $($body)*} };
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    // inline closure
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    ([$($captures:tt)*] $($rest:tt)*) => {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)            $crate::__cpp_internal!{ @find_rust_macro [] $($rest)*}
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            #[allow(unused)]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            #[derive($crate::__cpp_internal_closure)]
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            enum CppClosureInput {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                Input = (stringify!([$($captures)*] $($rest)*), 0).1
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            __cpp_closure_impl![$($captures)*]
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        }
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    };
[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    // wrap unsafe
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    (unsafe $($tail:tt)*) => { unsafe { cpp!($($tail)*) } };
[269](https://docs.rs#269)}
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)#[doc(hidden)]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)pub trait CppTrait {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    type BaseType;
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    const ARRAY_SIZE: usize;
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    const CPP_TYPE: &'static str;
[276](https://docs.rs#276)}
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// This macro allows wrapping a relocatable C++ struct or class that might have
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// a destructor or copy constructor, implementing the `Drop` and `Clone` trait
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// appropriately.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// ```ignore
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// cpp_class!(pub unsafe struct MyClass as "MyClass");
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// impl MyClass {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///     fn new() -> Self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///         unsafe { cpp!([] -> MyClass as "MyClass" { return MyClass(); }) }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)///     }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)///     fn member_function(&self, param : i32) -> i32 {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)///         unsafe { cpp!([self as "const MyClass*", param as "int"] -> i32 as "int" {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///             return self->member_function(param);
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///         }) }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///     }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// ```
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// This will create a Rust struct `MyClass`, which has the same size and
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// alignment as the C++ class `MyClass`. It will also implement the `Drop` trait
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// calling the destructor, the `Clone` trait calling the copy constructor, if the
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// class is copyable (or `Copy` if it is trivially copyable), and `Default` if the class
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// is default constructible
[301](https://docs.rs#301)///
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// ## Derived Traits
[303](https://docs.rs#303)///
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// The `Default`, `Clone` and `Copy` traits are implicitly implemented if the C++
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// type has the corresponding constructors.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// You can add the `#[derive(...)]` attribute in the macro in order to get automatic
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// implementation of the following traits:
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// * The trait `PartialEq` will call the C++ `operator==`.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// * You can add the trait `Eq` if the semantics of the C++ operator are those of `Eq`
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// * The trait `PartialOrd` need the C++ `operator<` for that type. `lt`, `le`, `gt` and
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///   `ge` will use the corresponding C++ operator if it is defined, otherwise it will
[314](https://docs.rs#314)///   fallback to the less than operator. For PartialOrd::partial_cmp, the `operator<` will
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///   be called twice. Note that it will never return `None`.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// * The trait `Ord` can also be specified when the semantics of the `operator<` corresponds
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///   to a total order
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// ## Safety Warning
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// Use of this macro is highly unsafe. Only certain C++ classes can be bound
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// to, C++ classes may perform arbitrary unsafe operations, and invariants are
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// easy to break.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// A notable restriction is that this macro only works if the C++ class is
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// relocatable.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// ## Relocatable classes
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// In order to be able to we wrapped the C++ class must be relocatable. That means
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// that it can be moved in memory using `memcpy`. This restriction exists because
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// safe Rust is allowed to move your types around.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)///
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// Most C++ types which do not contain self-references will be compatible,
[335](https://docs.rs#335)/// although this property cannot be statically checked by `rust-cpp`.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// All types that satisfy `std::is_trivially_copyable` are compatible.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)/// Maybe future version of the C++ standard would allow a compile-time check:
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// [P1144](http://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p1144r4.html)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// Unfortunately, as the STL often uses internal self-references for
[341](https://docs.rs#341)/// optimization purposes, such as the small-string optimization, this disallows
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// most std:: classes.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// But `std::unique_ptr<T>` and `std::shared_ptr<T>` works.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)#[macro_export]
[346](https://docs.rs#346)macro_rules! cpp_class {
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    };
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [pub] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    };
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub($($pub:tt)*) unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse [ $(#[$($attrs)*])* ] [pub($($pub)*)] [unsafe struct $name as $type] }
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    };
[356](https://docs.rs#356)}
[357](https://docs.rs#357)
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// Implementation details for cpp_class!
[359](https://docs.rs#359)#[doc(hidden)]
[360](https://docs.rs#360)#[macro_export]
[361](https://docs.rs#361)macro_rules! __cpp_class_internal {
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    (@parse [$($attrs:tt)*] [$($vis:tt)*] [unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr]) => {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes [ $($attrs)* ] [] [
[364](https://docs.rs#364)            #[derive($crate::__cpp_internal_class)]
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            #[repr(C)]
[366](https://docs.rs#366)            $($vis)* struct $name {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)                _opaque : [<$name as $crate::CppTrait>::BaseType ; <$name as $crate::CppTrait>::ARRAY_SIZE
[368](https://docs.rs#368)                    + (stringify!($($attrs)* $($vis)* unsafe struct $name as $type), 0).1]
[369](https://docs.rs#369)            }
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        ]}
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    };
[372](https://docs.rs#372)
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    (@parse_attributes [] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*]) => ( $($attributes)* $($result)* );
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    (@parse_attributes [#[derive($($der:ident),*)] $($tail:tt)* ] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*] )
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($der),*] @parse_attributes [$($tail)*] [ $($attributes)* ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    (@parse_attributes [ #[$m:meta] $($tail:tt)* ] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*])
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes [$($tail)*] [$($attributes)* #[$m] ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    (@parse_derive [] @parse_attributes $($result:tt)*) => ($crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_attributes $($result)*} );
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    (@parse_derive [PartialEq $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    (@parse_derive [PartialOrd $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    (@parse_derive [Ord $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    (@parse_derive [Default $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    (@parse_derive [Clone $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    (@parse_derive [Copy $(,$tail:ident)*] $($result:tt)*)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] $($result)*} );
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    (@parse_derive [$i:ident $(,$tail:ident)*] @parse_attributes [$($attr:tt)*] [$($attributes:tt)*] [$($result:tt)*] )
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        => ( $crate::__cpp_class_internal!{@parse_derive [$($tail),*] @parse_attributes [$($attr)*] [$($attributes)* #[derive($i)] ] [ $($result)* ] } );
[394](https://docs.rs#394)}

# cpp in cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cpp/macro.cpp.html

```
macro_rules! cpp {
    ({$($body:tt)*}) => { ... };
    ([$($captures:tt)*] $($rest:tt)*) => { ... };
    (unsafe $($tail:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

This macro is used to embed arbitrary C++ code.

There are two variants of the `cpp!` macro. The first variant is used for
raw text inclusion. Text is included into the generated `C++` file in the
order which they were defined, inlining module declarations.

The second variant is used to embed C++ code within Rust code. A list of variable names which should be captured are taken as the first argument, with their corresponding C++ type. The body is compiled as a C++ function.

This variant of the macro may only be invoked in expression context, and
requires an `unsafe` block, as it is performing FFI.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let y: i32 = 10;
let mut z: i32 = 20;
let x: i32 = unsafe { cpp!([y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
    z++;
    return y + z;
})};
```
You can also put the unsafe keyword as the first keyword of the `cpp!` macro, which
has the same effect as putting the whole macro in an `unsafe` block:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let x: i32 = cpp!(unsafe [y as "int32_t", mut z as "int32_t"] -> i32 as "int32_t" {
    z++;
    return y + z;
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-pseudo-macro)rust! pseudo-macro

The `cpp!` macro can contain, in the C++ code, a `rust!` sub-macro, which allows
the inclusion of Rust code in C++ code. This is useful to
implement callback or override virtual functions. Example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
trait MyTrait {
   fn compute_value(&self, x : i32) -> i32;
}
cpp!{{
   struct TraitPtr { void *a,*b; };
   class MyClassImpl : public MyClass {
     public:
       TraitPtr m_trait;
       int computeValue(int x) const override {
           return rust!(MCI_computeValue [m_trait : &MyTrait as "TraitPtr", x : i32 as "int"]
               -> i32 as "int" {
               m_trait.compute_value(x)
           });
       }
   }
}}
```
The syntax for the `rust!` macro is:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
rust!($uniq_ident:ident [$($arg_name:ident : $arg_rust_type:ty as $arg_c_type:tt),*]
     $(-> $ret_rust_type:ty as $rust_c_type:tt)* {$($body:tt)*})
```
`uniq_ident` is a unique identifier which will be used to name the `extern` function

---

# cpp_class in cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cpp/macro.cpp_class.html

```
macro_rules! cpp_class {
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
    ($(#[$($attrs:tt)*])* pub($($pub:tt)*) unsafe struct $name:ident as $type:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

This macro allows wrapping a relocatable C++ struct or class that might have
a destructor or copy constructor, implementing the `Drop` and `Clone` trait
appropriately.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
cpp_class!(pub unsafe struct MyClass as "MyClass");
impl MyClass {
    fn new() -> Self {
        unsafe { cpp!([] -> MyClass as "MyClass" { return MyClass(); }) }
    }
    fn member_function(&self, param : i32) -> i32 {
        unsafe { cpp!([self as "const MyClass*", param as "int"] -> i32 as "int" {
            return self->member_function(param);
        }) }
    }
}
```
This will create a Rust struct `MyClass`, which has the same size and
alignment as the C++ class `MyClass`. It will also implement the `Drop` trait
calling the destructor, the `Clone` trait calling the copy constructor, if the
class is copyable (or `Copy` if it is trivially copyable), and `Default` if the class
is default constructible

[§](https://docs.rs#derived-traits)Derived Traits

The `Default`, `Clone` and `Copy` traits are implicitly implemented if the C++
type has the corresponding constructors.

You can add the `#[derive(...)]` attribute in the macro in order to get automatic
implementation of the following traits:

- The trait `PartialEq`will call the C++`operator==`.
- You can add the trait `Eq`if the semantics of the C++ operator are those of`Eq`
- The trait `PartialOrd`need the C++`operator<`for that type.`lt`,`le`,`gt`and`ge`will use the corresponding C++ operator if it is defined, otherwise it will fallback to the less than operator. For PartialOrd::partial_cmp, the`operator<`will be called twice. Note that it will never return`None`.
- The trait `Ord`can also be specified when the semantics of the`operator<`corresponds to a total order

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-warning)Safety Warning

Use of this macro is highly unsafe. Only certain C++ classes can be bound to, C++ classes may perform arbitrary unsafe operations, and invariants are easy to break.

A notable restriction is that this macro only works if the C++ class is relocatable.

[§](https://docs.rs#relocatable-classes)Relocatable classes

In order to be able to we wrapped the C++ class must be relocatable. That means
that it can be moved in memory using `memcpy`. This restriction exists because
safe Rust is allowed to move your types around.

Most C++ types which do not contain self-references will be compatible,
although this property cannot be statically checked by `rust-cpp`.
All types that satisfy `std::is_trivially_copyable` are compatible.
Maybe future version of the C++ standard would allow a compile-time check:
[P1144](http://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p1144r4.html)

Unfortunately, as the STL often uses internal self-references for
optimization purposes, such as the small-string optimization, this disallows
most std:: classes.
But `std::unique_ptr<T>` and `std::shared_ptr<T>` works.

---

# cpp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cpp/latest/target-redirect/cpp/index.html

## Expand description

This crate `cpp` provides macros that allow embedding arbitrary C++ code.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This crate must be used in tandem with the [ cpp_build](https://docs.rs/cpp_build) crate. A basic Cargo
project which uses these projects would have a structure like the following:

```
crate
|-- Cargo.toml
|-- src
    |-- main.rs
|-- build.rs
```
Where the files look like the following:

[§](https://docs.rs#cargotoml)Cargo.toml

```
[package]
build = "build.rs"
[dependencies]
cpp = "0.5"
[build-dependencies]
cpp_build = "0.5"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#buildrs)build.rs

```
extern crate cpp_build;
fn main() {
    cpp_build::build("src/main.rs");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mainrs)main.rs

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use cpp::cpp;
cpp!{{
    #include <iostream>
}}
fn main() {
    let name = std::ffi::CString::new("World").unwrap();
    let name_ptr = name.as_ptr();
    let r = unsafe {
        cpp!([name_ptr as "const char *"] -> u32 as "int32_t" {
            std::cout << "Hello, " << name_ptr << std::endl;
            return 42;
        })
    };
    assert_eq!(r, 42)
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#build-script)Build script

Use the `cpp_build` crates from your `build.rs` script.
The same version of `cpp_build` and `cpp` crates should be used.
You can simply use the `cpp_build::build` function, or the `cpp_build::Config`
struct if you want more option.

Behind the scene, it uses the `cc` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-external-libraries)Using external libraries

Most likely you will want to link against external libraries. You need to tell cpp_build
about the include path and other flags via `cpp_build::Config` and you need to let cargo
know about the link. More info in the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html).

Your `build.rs` could look like this:

```
fn main() {
    let include_path = "/usr/include/myexternallib";
    let lib_path = "/usr/lib/myexternallib";
    cpp_build::Config::new().include(include_path).build("src/lib.rs");
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-search={}", lib_path);
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-lib=myexternallib");
}
```
(But you probably want to allow to configure the path via environment variables or
find them using some external tool such as the `pkg-config` crate, instead of hardcoding
them in the source)

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

As with all procedure macro crates we also need to parse Rust source files to
extract C++ code. That leads to the fact that some of the language features
might not be supported in full. One example is the attributes. Only a limited
number of attributes is supported, namely: `#[path = "..."]` for `mod`
declarations to specify an alternative path to the module file and
`#[cfg(feature = "...")]` for `mod` declarations to conditionally include the
module into the parsing process. Please note that the latter is only supported
in its simplest form: straight-forward `feature = "..."` without any
additional conditions, `cfg!` macros are also not supported at the moment.

Since the C++ code is included within a rust file, the C++ code must obey both
the Rust and the C++ lexing rules. For example, Rust supports nested block comments
(`/* ... /* ... */ ... */`) while C++ does not, so nested comments not be used in the
`cpp!` macro. Also the Rust lexer will not understand the C++ raw literal, nor all
the C++ escape sequences within literal, so only string literals that are both valid
in Rust and in C++ should be used. The same applies for group separators in numbers.
Be careful to properly use `#if` / `#else` / `#endif`, and not have unbalanced delimiters.

---
